I am the creator and lead developer of an open-source, edge-native headless CMS, and I have hands-on experience building computer vision applications and NLP-based recommendation algorithms.
summary:
During deep-space missions, communication delays make real-time medical support from Earth extremely difficult. In order to solve this problem, our team developed ARES-3, an autonomous biomedical monitoring system that utilizes an environmental physics engine, an unsupervised Deep Learning ECG Autoencoder, and an interactive dashboard.
Built around official NASA human-system standards (NASA-STD-3001), ARES-3 tracks crew vital signs, metabolic reintegration (which helps prevent bone density loss and muscle catabolism), and life-support parameters inside the ISS and EVA suits, including O2, CO2, barometric pressure, and radiation levels.
By comparing environmental conditions with physiological data, ARES-3 avoids false alarms during physical activities while detecting real emergencies, from cardiac arrhythmias to oxygen deficiency. It also tracks daily hydration and caloric intake, recommending specific corrective actions whenever an astronaut's values fall outside NASA space physiology guidelines while also keeping track of the subject's exposition to radiation. ARES-3 acts as an onboard first responder, which is practical and easy to understand, providing a direct point of contact between the medical personnel and the astronauts when ground support is delayed.
details: ARES-3 acts as a non-invasive health monitoring platform that tracks four crew members across pressurized station modules (habitat, laboratory, greenhouse, airlock) and Extravehicular Activities. It was built using Python (NumPy, Pandas, SciPy) for the deterministic physics engine, along with instruments such as TensorFlow/Keras for the machine learning model, and TypeScript for the interactive dashboard. Our system unifies environmental telemetry and wearable medical data into a single first responder. At its core, ARES-3 simulates collective cabin gas dynamics (O2 consumption, CO2 buildup, barometric pressure, and radiation levels) alongside individual vital signs, circadian rhythms, sleep stages, and hydration/caloric balance during daily routines and workouts on standard equipment. Simultaneously, an unsupervised Autoencoder trained exclusively on normal terrestrial heartbeats analyzes 140-sample ECG waveforms to detect real-time cardiac arrhythmias by measuring reconstruction error. Unlike standard medical equipment, ARES-3 was made as a multi-tool, capable of focusing on the single patient's needs while also monitoring the whole community, ensuring the entire team is working in a safe and optimal space. This, together with the versatility of the system, which could also be used to support other workers who operate in difficult environments, such as divers and mountain rescuers, makes ARES-3 excellent in translating raw data into life-saving procedures that can be easily understood by endangered workers.
